newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists would scrap pension law - Jospin.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists would scrap pension law - Jospin.

text.p: France's Socialist party would scrap a law passed in February introducing pension funds to France if it wins the parliamentary election, Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said on Monday.
"We are hostile to the law which was voted because it would threaten to destabilise the system of pensions via redistribution," he told a meeting in Brest, in Britanny.
"We will abolish these laws and if we have to make a place for complementary (pensions) it will be in a much more gradual way," he added.
Under the law, private pension funds will be introduced to complement the existing system of universal pensions, with tax benefits to encourage contributions to the pensions schemes.
:French Socialists will not sell or nationalise
By Jean-Michel Belot

PARIS, May 5 (Reuter) - The Socialists would return to their old policy of "neither privatisation nor nationalisation" if they won the French parliamentary election, the co-author of the party's economic manifesto pledged on Monday.
"We'll put a stop to this (conservative) programme of privatisation but we won't nationalise anything," Pierre Moscovici told Reuters.
When former Socialist President Francois Mitterrand was returned to (corrects) office in 1988, he introduced what was dubbed the "ni-ni" dogma -- no more privatisations, no more nationalisations.
"Our philosphy, in the end, is indeed the 'ni-ni' policy," Moscovici said in an interview.

The French vote in a two-round poll on May 25 and June 1. Conservative President Jacques Chirac called the snap election earlier this month, saying he needed to revitalise France for the introduction of a single European currency.
Recent polls have shown the race has tightened with the centre-right's lead over the Socialists shrinking.

"The Right's stand on public services, especially in its platform, means seeking maximum deregulation," he said. "We've got an attachment to public services, and to the idea there needs to be a pause in the privatisation process."

The Socialists were forced to backtrack on their anti-privatisation policy in 1991 under former Socialist prime minister Michel Rocard after the vast state-controlled sector grew so starved for capital that it could no longer afford to finance its growth without access to private sector funds.

Moscovici did not rule out implementing some of the policies adopted by Rocard in 1991 that allowed private firms, including foreign ones, to buy minority stakes in state-owned companies. "Alliances with foreigners remain absolutely possible," he said.

In 1993, when the centre-right came to power in French parliamentary elections, it abandoned the Socialists' privatisation policies, launching a drive to sell off some of the country's biggest state-owned companies.
A host have already either been partially or fully privatised including carmaker Renault, banks and insurers and computer maker Bull.
Moscovici reiterated the Socialist party's opposition to privatisation of state electronics firm Thomson-CSF and telephone giant France Telecom.
For Thomson-CSF, "we'll start all over again with the idea that this firm, which has returned to profit, should not be privatised," Moscovici said.

He said that if the Socialists took power, the party would have to make "an assessment of the public sector, and notably of the banking sector, in view of the fact we have not been managing affairs for four years."
The ruling centre-right plans to privatise state-owned bank Crdit Lyonnais, which went on an expansion spree in the late 1980s and early 1990s that almost led to its collapse.
The bank racked up 21 billion francs ($3.6 billion) in losses between 1992 and 1994 before limping back to profit in 1995, thanks to massive government handouts. ($ = 5.824 French Francs)
